Lives · c.1162–1227

Genghis Khan

Empire & Conquest · Mongolia · c.1162–1227

2 min readWhere it is contestedCorrected onceUpdated 19 September 2026
On this pageWhere it is contestedCorrectedThe definitive biographyReads across to

An outcast boy on the steppe who survived captivity and near-starvation, and founded the empire that his heirs made the largest contiguous land empire in history.

If you keep one line

Merit over bloodline was a weapon before it was a value.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

Born Temüjin, he united the warring nomadic tribes and built an empire stretching, at its height, from Korea to Hungary. The conquests were staggeringly violent; whole cities were erased. Yet to reduce him to a destroyer is to miss why historians keep returning to him.

He ran a meritocracy in an age of bloodlines, promoting commanders on ability rather than birth. He established a written Mongol script, guaranteed religious freedom across his domains, abolished torture as policy in places, protected diplomats and merchants, and stitched together a Eurasian trade and communication network — the Pax Mongolica — along which goods, technologies and ideas (paper, printing, gunpowder, the compass) flowed west and reshaped the world.

More than the borders he drew, it is this circulation of knowledge, and the genetic and cultural fingerprint he left across a continent, that makes the case for him as a maker of the modern world.

01Where it is contested

This is the most disputed pick on the shelf. Weatherford's revisionism is vivid and hugely influential in the popular view, but Mongol-studies specialists have criticised it as over-corrective, thin on some sources and prone to crediting the Mongols with developments that predate or postdate them. Read it against Timothy May or Christopher Atwood for the scholarly account.

02Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 15 · Sept 2026 · Six superlatives.

An audit of claims printed as 'first', 'only' or 'most' found six that said more than a source would. Genghis Khan's entry said he forged the largest contiguous land empire in history; it reached that size under his heirs, after his death in 1227. Rockefeller's called his the largest fortune in American history, with no measure attached; by inflation-adjusted wealth it is not, and by share of the economy it has arguably been overtaken. It now says one of the largest. Edward Thorp's said Beat the Dealer was, by his own description, the first book to prove the house edge could be beaten; his own account of the book does not say so. Why Firms Exist said Coase's paper was largely ignored for thirty years; the paper was cited long before it was put to use, and the entry now quotes only what Coase is on record as saying, that it was little more than an undergraduate essay. Maurice Hilleman's and Fritz Haber's entries stated as the house's own finding what are other people's judgments; both are now worded as such.

03The definitive biography

Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern WorldJack Weatherford · 2004

Drawing on the long-suppressed Secret History of the Mongols and years of fieldwork, Weatherford overturns the cartoon villain and argues for Genghis Khan as an unlikely modernizer.

04Reads across to

Napoleon Bonaparte — the other empire run on promotion by merit, and the other ledger of what it cost.

Ibn Khaldun — the theory of this life, written a century and a half later: a cohesive group from the steppe takes the cities, and the cities undo it.
